claims.text: Applying a dense, well-adherent CrN coating to boride-based components will significantly improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
Sputter deposition can produce a dense CrN coating on boride surfaces.
Temperatures of 700–750 °C are typical of hot-dip aluminum-plating exposure.
A continuous CrN layer will act as a diffusion barrier on the boride substrate.
The CrN layer will prevent direct chemical interaction between molten aluminum and the underlying boride substrate.
CrN inhibits aluminum penetration by limiting ion diffusion.
CrN suppresses the formation of deleterious reaction products such as aluminum-boride compounds.
Suppressing aluminum penetration and reaction-product formation will reduce corrosion of the boride component.
CrN-coated boride components will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than uncoated boride components under identical molten-aluminum exposure.
CrN-coated specimens will exhibit less weight loss after molten-aluminum exposure than uncoated specimens.
CrN-coated specimens will exhibit less surface degradation after molten-aluminum exposure than uncoated specimens.
The protective effect will persist while the CrN coating maintains its integrity and adhesion.
Extreme thermal cycling, mechanical damage, or temperatures above the CrN coating's stability limit could compromise protection.
The optimum coating thickness and exact deposition parameters remain undetermined.
The long-term behavior of CrN under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses remains undetermined.
A controlled comparison of coated and uncoated identical components under the same molten-aluminum immersion conditions can test the hypothesis.
Failure of the coated specimens to show a statistically significant reduction in corrosion rate and surface degradation relative to uncoated controls would falsify the hypothesis.
